messages.subject: Re: Run parallel chains and update model
messages.subject_clean: Run parallel chains and update model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Quresh,

It's probably picking up the value of `nspp` from a variable named `nspp` in your R global environment when it is not found in `constants`. That variable wouldn't be present in the worker processes, hence the error when parallelizing.

In some cases, we've been careful to prevent objects from being found via R's scoping rules, but in this case and some other cases, objects will be found by R's scoping rules if you don't provide them in the usual 'nimble' manner. In this case, it might be better if nimble errored out -- it's something that's been in the back of our minds for a while.

-chris

On Tue, Dec 27, 2022 at 2:16 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> Well, once I sat down at my desk for real and my brain wasn't in vacation mode, I quickly found the error in my code. I had not included 'nspp' in my list of constants. The 'nspp' object specifies the number of species represented in the data, and thus the length of the species loop for defining the model. Given the bone-headed nature of my mistake, I now feel sheepish posting about it here, except that it's still puzzling why the model ran with 'nimbleMCMC' without throwing an error. I also was able to run the model using the more base set of NIMBLE functions that are embedded within 'RunNimbleParallel' (i.e., nimbleModel, compileNimble, configureMCMC, etc. implemented in lines 24 to 32 in the 'RunNimbleParallel' function). The model and samplers apparently get compiled and run just fine with no errors even though I am missing 'nspp' in my list of constants. Moreover, when I check the model after defining it using the 'nimbleModel' function by running 'model$calculate()', I get a number rather than NA or Inf, so the log-probability appears fully defined despite not having specified the length of the species loop. Curious if there are any insights out there as to why I only get an error with this mistake when attempting parallel processing.
>
> On Sunday, December 25, 2022 at 1:30:25 PM UTC-7 Quresh Latif wrote:
> > Hi all. I have run into a headscratcher with the parallel processing function that I wrote and posted in this thread. I am trying to run a zero-inflated dynamic community abundance model. The model runs fine with 'nimbleMCMC', but when I try to run it using ' RunNimbleParallel' function, I get the following error:
> >
> > "Error in checkForRemoteErrors(lapply(cl, recvResult)) : 2 nodes produced errors; first error: Could not evaluate loop syntax: is indexing information provided via 'constants'?"
> >
> > A zip file containing a somewhat stripped down version of the model (no covariates), along with data in an R workspace and scripts for running the model both with 'nimbleMCMC' and 'RunNimbleParallel' is posted here <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1f764N4lleNuYu5lG_9ocJz8kgAvOaTAy/view?usp=share_link>. I suspect it has something to do with the multi-species aspect of the model since a single species version runs just fine, but it's not yet clear to me what's wrong with my indexing, especially since the model runs fine using 'nimbleMCMC'. I am still working on stripping the model down further to see if I can clearly isolate the component that isn't incompatible with my parallelization function, but just thought I'd post what I've got so far in case anyone has the time and interest to help me troubleshoot. I'd especially be curious to know if anyone else is able to run this model using the 'RunNimbleParallel' function, or if they get the same error in their environment as I know that parallelization functions can be sensitive to the operating system.
> >
> > Appreciate any thoughts or suggestions from anyone.
> >

messages.subject: Bayesian Analysis for Penalized Spline Regression
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian Analysis for Penalized Spline Regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear NIMBLE authors,

I was trying to replicate a very basic analysis of a penalized spline regression, described in a paper titled "Bayesian Analysis for Penalized Spline Regression Using WinBUGS" (see  https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v014i14). As it works by WinBUGS, I wonder if NIMBLE can replicate the results therein. I obtained the data from the `SemiPar` package, though the data seem a bit different from the scatter plot.

I have attached the NIMBLE syntax that tries to replicate the age-income example. However, the results are quite different from Table 1. I also compared my NIMBLE syntax with the WinBUGS syntax in the paper but didn't find any marked difference.

I am not sure that the difference results from the NIMBLE or anything I missed. Hope you could help to have a look at this issue.

Thank you for the excellent NIMBLE package!

Best wishes,
Keith

messages.body_plain:
I notice that the paper gave initial values of `b` with all zeros, so I tried it again. I ran longer and multiple chains, and plotted the trace (see the attached R code). The `beta` parameters seem to be difficult to converge, which is odd. WinBUGS seems to give a similar phenomenon to NIMBLE. Although now NIMBLE gave results closer to the paper. It may mean that this spline regression model is very sensitive to initial values and unstable.

The warning message here came from your choice of initial values for latent ~ dcat(pi). Given other initial values, the value of pi is (0, 0, 0, 1) for each i but your initial value for latent is 1. If you use 4 as the initial value for latent, the code will run fine without that warning. Hope it helps.

Best wishes,
Wei

Hi all,

I am running into an error when compiling models under NIMBLE 0.13.1.      mu ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)

         x[i] ~ dnorm(mu, sd = sigma)

Hmm, could you try to see if a basic Rcpp invocation works to see if this is a nimble issue. E.g.,

```
Rcpp::cppFunction(
          'int fibonacci(const int x) {
              if (x == 0) return(0);
              if (x == 1) return(1);
              return (fibonacci(x - 1)) + fibonacci(x - 2);
          }')

fibonacci(7)
```

Also, from your PATH it looks like you have both Rtools 42 and Rtools 40 installed. You may want to remove 40.

Finally, there's a similar error report using Stan from R: https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstanr/issues/699.
There are some suggestions there of things to try related to PATH.

messages.subject: Re: Missing data in multinomial distribution
messages.subject_clean: Missing data in multinomial distribution
messages.body_plain:
hi Abigail,

I haven't looked closely at this, but the first thing to modify is that the obs_ref, no_m, nad no_f inputs to calc_cond_prob in your model declaration are vectors and need to be given as such (i.e., with brackets), such as:

pic_trap[1:ntime,1:nobs,1:nsite] <- calc_cond_prob(nsite,ntime,nobs,obs_ref[1:X,1:Y,1:Z],p_m,p_f,no_m[1:W,1:U],no_f[1:T,1:S])

where you'll need to change 1:X, 1:Y, ..., 1:S, to be the right values for your context.

The warning messages are trying to say this (by indicating that obs_ref is a scalar in the model but provided as a non-scalar to the model), but they are a bit hard to decipher.

Also, all model variables are treated internally as doubles (i.e., double precision floating point), so you'll want to have the arguments for your nimble function be double rather than integer. This won't be a problem, since it's fine to store integer-valued numbers as doubles.

The main issue, though, is that I don't think having NAs in your multinomial obs vector will work - it will produce an NA in your likelihood. This will probably be a larger discussion and others may weigh in. One option may be to set up the multinomial as a set of sequential binomials (also called stick-breaking) and impute the missing values in the MCMC. Another would be to use some trickery with nimbleFunctions to sample the missing elements of the multinomial but that would probably take some work. I'm not fully seeing what different possible y vectors you can have... e.g., if you have a single NA, then you actually know that value because the elements have to sum to the multinomial total.

-chris

On Thu, Jan 12, 2023 at 5:15 PM Abigail Keller <agke...@berkeley.edu> wrote:

> Hi -- I'm new to NIMBLE, so I apologize for these likely basic questions. I'm trying to figure out the best way to handle missing observations in a multinomial distribution of invasive species removal count data.
>
> I have an array of count data indexed by time, removal observation, and site (y[t,j,i]), and there are inconsistent numbers of removal observations from each site at each time point (missing count data marked as NA in the array). There are two removal methods, denoted "m" and "f". I want these count data to be drawn from a multinomial distribution, where the cell probabilities are the probability of being captured by each removal method (p_m and p_f), conditional upon the probability of being captured at all. For example, if y[t,j,i] was captured with removal type m, the conditional probability would be:
> pi_c[t,j,i] = p_m / (total_m_obs[t,i]*p_m + total_f_obs[t,i]*p_f)
>
> And then if y[t,j,i] = NA, then pi_c[t,j,i] = NA.
>
> Here is the code I have been trying:
>
> constants <- list(nsite = dim(DH2020_all_count)[3], #scalar, number of sites, i
>                   ntime = dim(DH2020_all_count)[1], #scalar, max number of time periods, t
>                   nobs = dim(DH2020_all_count)[2], #scalar, max number of removal observations, j
>                   no_f = no_f, #matrix w/ dimensions [t,i] of number of removal observations, type f
>                   no_m = no_m, #matrix w/ dimensions [t,i] of number of removal observations, type m
>                   obs_ref = DH2020_all_trap_ref) #array [t,j,i] indexing the type of removal observation ("M", "F", or NA for missing)
>
> data <- list(n_cap = n_cap, #matrix w/ dimensions [t,i] total count removed
>              y = DH2020_all_count) #array w/ dimensions [t,j,i] for count removed, contains NAs
>
> #write function for calculating conditional probabilities with missing data
> calc_cond_prob <- nimbleFunction(
>   #input and output types
>   run = function(nsite = integer(0), # scalar
>                  ntime = integer(0), # scalar
>                  nobs = integer(0), # scalar
>                  obs_ref = integer(3),  # array
>                  p_m = double(0), #scalar
>                  p_f = double(0), # scalar
>                  no_m = integer(2), # matrix
>                  no_f = integer(2)) #matrix
>     {
>     returnType(double(3))  # array return

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to develop an MCMC model that involves fitting an AR1 model to a timeseries of data for each of N grid cells. Here is what I have so far (apologies if it is way off base):

library(nimble)

source('dlik.R') # contents of this file are below

N = 40 # grid cells

m = 65 # time steps (years) in timeseries

truth_residuals = matrix(rnorm(N*m,sd=1),N,m) # sample data to fit AR1 parameters to

sample_rho                       = matrix(rnorm(N*10000,sd=1),N,10000)

sample_rho[sample_rho >= 0.999]  = 0.999

sample_rho[sample_rho <= -0.999] = -0.999

sample_sigma                       = matrix(rnorm(N*10000,sd=1),N,10000)

sample_sigma[sample_sigma <= 0.01] = 0.01

Rcode <- nimbleCode({

  # likelihood ==============

  for(i in 1:N) Y[i,1:m] ~ dar1(sigma=sigma0[i],rho=rho0[i])

  # process =================

  for (i in 1:N) sigma0[i] ~ dunif(0.01,max(sigma.all))

  for (i in 1:N) rho0[i] ~ dunif(-0.999,0.999)

})

# Set up model

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(

  code = Rcode,

  constants = list(N = N, m = m),                                                 # Specify constants (fixed, non-data quantities)

  inits = list(sigma0=apply(sample_sigma,1,mean),rho0=apply(sample_rho,1,mean)),  # initial values for sigma and rho

  data = list( Y = truth_residuals)

)

comp <- compileNimble(Rmodel,showCompilerOutput = TRUE)                    # Compile the model

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)                                              # Configure the model

conf$printSamplers()

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)                                                   # Build the MCMC

Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel,showCompilerOutput = TRUE)  # Compile the MCMC in C++

samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc,niter=1e5,nchains=1)

# dlik.R

# User-defined nimbleFunction for the AR1 distribution

dar1 <- nimbleFunction(

  run = function( x = double(1), sigma = double(0), rho = double(0),

                  log = integer(0, default = 0) ) {

    returnType(double(0))

    m <- length(x)

    w <- x[2:m] - rho*x[1:(m-1)]      # whitened residuals

    sigma.proc <- sigma/sqrt(1-rho^2) # stationary process variance sigma.proc^2

    logdens <- dnorm(x[1],sd=sigma.proc,log=TRUE) + sum(dnorm(w,sd=sigma,log=TRUE))

    if( log ){ return( logdens ) }

    else{ return( exp( logdens ) ) }

})

rar1 <- nimbleFunction(

  run = function(n = integer(0, default = 1),

                 sigma = double(0), rho = double(0) ) {

    returnType(double(0))

    return(1)

})

registerDistributions( list(dar1 = list(

  BUGSdist = "dar1(sigma, rho)",

  types = c("sigma = double(0)", "rho = double(0)")

)))

I'm getting the error "Dimension of distribution argument(s) 'value' does not match required dimension(s) for the distribution 'dar1'. Necessary dimension(s) are 0." More generally I'm pretty sure I'm treating the spatiotemporal nature of the data incorrectly and would appreciate some guidance on the matter.

messages.subject: Re: loo package for NIMBLE
messages.subject_clean: loo package for NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
A rather belated reply, perhaps mostly for posterity. One option would be to save the logProb values for the data points by monitoring them (e.g., if `y` is the variable containing the observations, you would monitor `logProb_y`). Then you could concatenate the output from multiple chains and provide the logProb values for the responses to `loo::waic`, rather than using `calculateWAIC`. Of course this is only viable if you don't have so many observations and MCMC samples that you use too much memory in saving all the logProb values. And if saving all the observation logProbs is viable, then monitoring all needed nodes will generally be viable as well (and use less memory).

On Tuesday, June 14, 2022 at 8:58:04 PM UTC-7 Keith Lau wrote:
> Thank you for your time and the reply, Chris and John. I've followed John's instructions and confirmed that the loo package had the same offline WAIC results.
>
> Off the point: It took me a while to get the results because I used parallel computation. As shown at https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/nSNLN7LA2dk , it requires a lot of computer memory for my model to collect all the nodes, compile the model again, and use calculateWAIC(). In comparison, to use loo package, I just need to collect the logProb_response (log likelihood for each data point) and use loo::waic() to get the same offline WAIC, which saved a lot of computer memory. It seems the parallel nimble for WAIC has no simple way to get yet (?).
>
> John Clare 在 2022年6月5日 星期日凌晨2:32:58 [UTC+8] 的信中寫道：
> > Hi Keith,
> >
> > loo::loo or loo::waic is simply looking for an n_posterior_samples * n_observations (observation constituting whatever unit is germane to the likelihood)  matrix of log (y|parameters), or n_posterior_samples_per_chain* n_observations*n_chains array. This can be generated within the nimble model itself using something like:
> >
> > for (i in 1:n){
> >  y[i]~dnorm(mu, sd=sigma)
> > loglike[i]<-dnorm(y[i], mu, sd=sigma, log=1)
> > }
> > ...
> >
> > where you'd trace "loglike". If you store all of the germane parameters (above, mu/sigma), you can also calculate this after the fact--a non-optimized example might have the following r loop:
> > loglike<-matrix(NA, nsamps, n)
> > for (i in 1:n){
> >   for (s in 1:nrow(samps)){
> >     loglike[s,i]<-dnorm(y[i], samps$mu[s], sd=samps$sigma[s], log=TRUE)
> >  }
> > }
> >
> > Could create and compile a nimble function that does something like the above, which could be useful for using varied existing nimble functions or distributions or speeding things up.
> >
> > You can also pass a function (perhaps compiled) to loo::waic that itself calls the germane data and iterative parameters and generates a matrix of log likelihood values that the subsequent waic calculations employ. loo::waic(x=<function>) requires data and parameters to be formatted in a certain way.
> >
> > John

> > > Hello everyone,
> > >
> > > I'm looking for an example of using loo package  <https://mc-stan.org/users/interfaces/loo>to obtain leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation and WAIC. I searched the internet but seemed no exact examples found. Could anyone indicate or provide examples?

Hi,

I just transferred my JAGS code of modeling the multinomial probabilities into NIMBLE. I have confirmed that my NIMBLE installation steps are correct, but it still reports "Error: Failed to create the shared library." I have also tried a similar Binomial model. It CAN work in NIMBLE without any errors. So, I just wonder which step in this multinomial version code might involve issues.

I want to ask for your helps about troubleshooting. A runnable sample code is provided below. I will appreciate a lot if anyone wants to have a try and share some ideas about any potential problems :)

#some data and constants

N <- rep(100, 30)
study <- rep(1:15, each=2)
trt <- c(rep(c(1,2), 5), rep(c(1,3), 5), rep(c(2,3), 5))

# model building
model <- nimbleCode({
  for (j in 1:J){
    Y[j,1:3] ~ dmulti(theta.adj[j,1:3], N[j])

    theta.adj[j,1:3] <- max(0.00001, min(theta[j,1:3], 0.99999))

    theta[j,1] <- 1/(1+rr21[j]+rr31[j])
    theta[j,2] <- rr21[j]/(1+rr21[j]+rr31[j])
    theta[j,3] <- rr31[j]/(1+rr21[j]+rr31[j])

    log(rr21[j]) <- alpha1[study[j]] + beta1[trt[j]]
    log(rr31[j]) <- alpha2[study[j]] + beta2[trt[j]]
  }
  #prior specifications
  for (i1 in 1:n.study){
    alpha1[i1] ~ dnorm(mu.study1, sd=sigma.study1)
    alpha2[i1] ~ dnorm(mu.study2, sd=sigma.study2)
  }
  mu.study1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
  mu.study2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
  sigma.study1 ~ T(dt(0, a, 1), 0,)
  sigma.study2 ~ T(dt(0, a, 1), 0,)

  for (i2 in 1:n.trt){
    beta1[i2] ~ dnorm(mu.trt1, sd=sigma.trt1)
    beta2[i2] ~ dnorm(mu.trt2, sd=sigma.trt2)
  }
  mu.trt1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
  mu.trt2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
  sigma.trt1 ~ T(dt(0, a, 1), 0,)
  sigma.trt2 ~ T(dt(0, a, 1), 0,)

  rr21_ov <- exp( mean(alpha1[1:n.study]) + mean(beta1[1:n.trt]) )
  rr31_ov <- exp( mean(alpha2[1:n.study]) + mean(beta2[1:n.trt]) )
  p1_ov <- 1/(1+rr21_ov+rr31_ov)
  p2_ov <- rr21_ov/(1+rr21_ov+rr31_ov)
  p3_ov <- rr31_ov/(1+rr21_ov+rr31_ov)
})

consts <- list(N=N, J=30, study=study, trt=trt,
               a=0.0016, n.study=15, n.trt=3)
data <- list(Y=Y)
initials <- list(alpha1=rep(-1, 15), mu.study1=-1, sigma.study1=0.05,

rModel <- nimbleModel(code=model, data=data, inits=initials, constants=consts)

cModel <- compileNimble(rModel)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

Thanks for the question.  Although we try to catch errors before they become C++ compilation errors, we can't catch them all.  The C++ error, while mostly unreadable, says the error is in "theta_dot_adj_L3", which is a converted name for theta.dot from line 3 of the code.

I believe the problem is in

theta.adj[j,1:3] <- max(0.00001, min(theta[j,1:3], 0.99999))

nimble's compilable version of max and min do not support arbitrary arguments (a vector, then a scalar) as R's versions do.  In addition, types are strict, which in this case means you can't assign a scalar to a vector. And also I am not sure if you want a vectorized operation of the max and min or not.  If you want a scalar result, so that theta.adj[j,1:3] has the same value repeated 3 times, please try

theta.adj[j,1:3] <- rep(max(0.00001, min(c(theta[j,1:3], 0.99999))), 3)
or, equivalently
theta.adj[j,1:3] <- rep(max(0.00001, min(min(theta[j,1:3]), 0.99999)), 3)

If you want a vector result, doing the max-min element-wise to theta[j, 1:3], please try

theta.adj[j,1:3] <- pmax(0.00001, pmin(theta[j,1:3], 0.99999))

If you still have problems (and I haven't tested the code I'm suggesting so could be making a mistake), please try making a simplified model with only the single line like this to experiment with it, and post again if you're still stuck.

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bill,

CPO uses leave-one-out fitting, so it's not something we provide directly in NIMBLE. You could of course program it, but fitting all the MCMCs as a brute force approach would of course be computationally demanding.

-chris

Is it typical for the intercept and covariate parameters for a given demographic parameter to be correlated and therefore good candidates for trying a RW_block sampler to sample them together?

I have an exponential growth parameter, r, in a population model that I am relating with covariates using a log link function:

log(r[g, (t-1)]) <- delta0 + inprod(deltaVec[1:n.Xdelta], Xdelta.array[g, t, 1:n.Xdelta]), where g indexes site and t indexes year.

I've got a couple traceplot (after applying some burnin and thinning) shown in the attached images, one for the intercept (delta0) and the other for the 12th covariate (delta12). The traceplots for the other covariate parameters look similar where the black chain looks to be mixing reasonably well but the red one is struggling. Considering these, does it seem like the log-linear regression parameters for r are likely correlated and would benefit from an RW_block sampler?

Also, I am currently using adaptation. I'm wondering if there's a way to record the tuning values ('scale' in the configureMCMC function?) or if that is automatically recorded somewhere. If so, would it help to identify what scale has arrived at for the black chain and then fix it to that value from the beginning for both chains? Along with that, is it possible to set 'scale' to different values for different parameters, or somehow tune the samplers for different parameters differently?

I am still working through the section of the user manual on this, so apologies for taking up space here if this is all spelled out there.

A categorical sampler for a node with many categories can be inefficient, and that node may not be a limitation on mixing, so it can work well to use a faster sampler.  Sometimes multiple nodes share identical or nearly identical dependencies (other nodes that depend on them).  This means that the same computational effort is involved in sampling them, and for this reason it can make sense to sample them jointly, such as with RW_block.  Sometimes we can identify parts of a model that can be re-written using nimbleFunctions to provide new functions or distributions in the model.  New functions can combine multiple steps into single steps, reducing the size of the model, which can improve efficiency.  New distributions can be useful to analytically sum or integrate over latent states when it is simple to do so.  The zero-inflated Poisson example on our web site is a simple case.  More complicated cases of doing this for capture-recapture and hidden Markov models are given in Turek et al. (2016; Environ Ecol Stat (2016) 23: 549. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-016-0353-z). messages.body_plain:
Hey Quresh,
I had this happen in a non-demographic model a few years ago. A block update didn't help (but this was using my own MCMC sampler). I ended up fixing it by using hierarchical standardizing.

I isolated this as the potential issue by plotting histograms of the mean-centered covariates and realizing that for the individuals with high correlation between the intercept and a coefficient, the corresponding covariate was not actually mean centered. The further off it was from mean=0 the worse the correlation in the chains. Then I replicated the problem with simulated data. It does change your interpretation of the coefficients a bit.

A few years later Kiona Ogle published this paper which talks about the same issue: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/eap.2159.

Maybe just something to check for in your covariates, if it's relevant for your type of hierarchical model.
-Franny

messages.subject: "Failed to create the shared library" error on USGS supercomputer
messages.subject_clean: "Failed to create the shared library" error on USGS supercomputer
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to run my Nimble chains in parallel on our supercomputer (USGS - Yeti). I've tried with parallel and with doParallel/foreach and I'm getting the same error with both: "Failed to create the shared library." It's referring to the parallel step in both cases (e.g., "Calls: %dopar% -> <Anonymous>" with foreach). This error *only sometimes occurs* - about 20-30% of the time, the job runs successfully (same job). It also occurs only when I try to submit the job through slurm on the supercomputer. It does not occur when I run it directly in R on the supercomputer, nor when I run it on my own laptop. Unfortunately, I can't run 'printErrors()' through slurm (the job aborts at the first error so nothing after that runs).

I've tried this in several versions of R (4.2.0 is the newest available on the supercomputer) with nimble 0.13.1. Let me know if more info on the Yeti configuration would be helpful.

Does anyone have any idea what might be causing this? Or does anyone happen to have example scripts they've used to successfully parallelize Nimble on USGS's Yeti supercomputer?

Here's a toy example that reproduces the error on Yeti (most of the time...). I'm sure this will run just fine on your system, so it may not be that helpful! The error doesn't occur if I comment out the runMCMC part.

library(nimble); library(foreach); library(doParallel)
options(stringsAsFactors=FALSE, scipen=10, digits=12, digits.secs=3)

mycode <- nimbleCode({
    y ~ dnorm(0,1)
})

# Set up a function to run nimble in parallel:
parMCMC <- function(X){
    mymodel <- nimbleModel(mycode)
    mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(mymodel)
    mcmcConf$setMonitors('y')
    mymcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
    compiled <- compileNimble(mymodel, mymcmc)
    myres <- runMCMC(compiled$mymcmc, niter=2000, nburnin=1000, nchains=1, thin=1, samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE, progressBar=F)
    return(myres)
}

# Run it:
cl <- makeCluster(3)
registerDoParallel(cl)
myresults <- foreach(i=1:3, .packages=c('nimble')) %dopar% {
    myres <- parMCMC(X=i)
    myres
}
stopCluster(cl)
registerDoSEQ()

Hi Suzy,

I hope this email finds you well!

If you see the first draws from the mcmc (remove burnin and thinning when doing mcmc.out) you can see that the 'b' and 'bm' variables are being updated. Very poor mixing though....

A few comments:
1. it seems that you are clustering columns and in your 'y' matrix data the columns are exactly the same. Is this what you want to do?
2. You are using a level of truncation for the stick breaking of size 4, which is way too small for this to be an approximation to the DP.

I hope this helps. Let me know if you have any other questions.

Best,
Claudia

messages.body_plain:
Hi. I am also getting this error. Based on the info here, it sounds like I might need to double check my initial values to make sure they have the correct dimensions, but before I do that, I wanted to make sure my coding is valid. I am doing this:

      model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model",
                           constants = constants, data = data,
                           inits = init)
      Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
      modelConf <- configureMCMC(model, thin = nt)
      modelConf$removeSamplers(c("delta0", "deltaVec[1:n.Xdelta]"))
      modelConf$addSampler(c("delta0", "deltaVec[1:n.Xdelta]"), type = "RW_block")
      modelConf$addMonitors(parameters)
      modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
      CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
      CmodelMCMC$run(ni, reset = FALSE)
      return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))

'n.Xdelta' is listed in 'constants'. Is it valid to use a constant to define the indexing of nodes for adding and removing samplers, or do I have to do that differently?

If I am not lost, I think this was from using nrow(dat$Abund) instead of ncol(dat$Abund) in the last step of OrdInits2D.  Having the wrong length inits for alSpeciesSTAR caused a cascade of issues into the block sampler for alSpeciesSTAR (or the one with it as a component).

messages.body_plain:
Quresh, briefly, I think you identified the issue, and I don't believe you can use the variable name "n.Xdelta" in your indexing of vector-valued nodes in calls to addSampler() or removeSamplers().  I think you'll need instead (if n.Xdelta=10, for example):

modelConf$removeSamplers(c("delta0", "deltaVec[1:10]"))

or, in the case that the *entirety* of "deltaVec" is in fact deltaVec[1:n.Xdelta], then you should be safe with:

modelConf$removeSamplers(c("delta0", "deltaVec"))

Could you give this a try, and let me know if this work?

Cheers,
Daniel

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily,

I suspect this is not anything related to nimble.

It sounds like it always fails on some nodes and succeeds on others. Given the error message about 'features.h' not being found, are you sure that 'features.h' exists on the node(s) where it fails? (That said, I would have guessed your IT support person would have checked that...)

I believe features.h should be located in /opt/ohpc/pub/compiler/gcc/8.3.0/include/c++/8.3.0/parallel/features.h on all the nodes. You could look manually or do this in your code before calling compileNimble:

file.exists("/opt/ohpc/pub/compiler/gcc/8.3.0/include/c++/8.3.0/parallel/features.h")

and see if existence of the file corresponds with success/failure.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

Regarding the error message, that is referring to the fact that 'x' should be a vector not a scalar, so you need `x = double(1)` when defining `dar1`.
We should clarify that error message - I've made a note for us to do that.

Also, you'll need  `Y[i,1:m]` in your model code.
And as a side note, you don't need `rar1` or `registerDistributions`, though it's ok to have them. As you have it ,`rar1` is not consistent with `dar1` as it returns a scalar, but it's just a placeholder, so it's ok.

Apart from that it should work from a mechanical perspective. Perhaps others will comment on your modeling question - it's a broad question and there are lots of things one can do with spatio-temporal data like this - allowing for spatial structure in 'y' or in 'sigma' or in 'rho'.

-Chris

> conf$printSamplers()

> samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc,niter=1e5,nchains=1)

>
> # dlik.R
>

Quresh, to address your question about the adapted scale parameters of the RW sampler, the vignette below should demonstrate what you're trying to do.  The facilities exist in the RW samplers, although these may not be well documented (or documented at all) in the User Manual.  Let me know if you have any questions about it:

danielturek.github.io/public/RWscaleHistory/RWscaleHistory.html <http://danielturek.github.io/public/RWscaleHistory/RWscaleHistory.html>

On Thu, Jan 19, 2023 at 6:52 PM fbud...@gmail.com <fbud...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hey Quresh,
> I had this happen in a non-demographic model a few years ago. A block update didn't help (but this was using my own MCMC sampler). I ended up fixing it by using hierarchical standardizing.
>
> I isolated this as the potential issue by plotting histograms of the mean-centered covariates and realizing that for the individuals with high correlation between the intercept and a coefficient, the corresponding covariate was not actually mean centered. The further off it was from mean=0 the worse the correlation in the chains. Then I replicated the problem with simulated data. It does change your interpretation of the coefficients a bit.
>
> A few years later Kiona Ogle published this paper which talks about the same issue: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/eap.2159.
>
> Maybe just something to check for in your covariates, if it's relevant for your type of hierarchical model.
> -Franny
>
>
>
> On Thursday, January 19, 2023 at 6:38:21 PM UTC-5 quresh...@birdconservancy.org wrote:
> > Is it typical for the intercept and covariate parameters for a given demographic parameter to be correlated and therefore good candidates for trying a RW_block sampler to sample them together?
> >
> > I have an exponential growth parameter, r, in a population model that I am relating with covariates using a log link function:
> >
> > log(r[g, (t-1)]) <- delta0 + inprod(deltaVec[1:n.Xdelta], Xdelta.array[g, t, 1:n.Xdelta]), where g indexes site and t indexes year.
> >
> > I've got a couple traceplot (after applying some burnin and thinning) shown in the attached images, one for the intercept (delta0) and the other for the 12th covariate (delta12). The traceplots for the other covariate parameters look similar where the black chain looks to be mixing reasonably well but the red one is struggling. Considering these, does it seem like the log-linear regression parameters for r are likely correlated and would benefit from an RW_block sampler?
> >
> > Also, I am currently using adaptation. I'm wondering if there's a way to record the tuning values ('scale' in the configureMCMC function?) or if that is automatically recorded somewhere. If so, would it help to identify what scale has arrived at for the black chain and then fix it to that value from the beginning for both chains? Along with that, is it possible to set 'scale' to different values for different parameters, or somehow tune the samplers for different parameters differently?
> >
> > I am still working through the section of the user manual on this, so apologies for taking up space here if this is all spelled out there.
> >
> > On Friday, March 1, 2019 at 9:47:36 AM UTC-7 pdevalpine wrote:
> > > I'll add some strategies to what Chris wrote.
> > >
> > > Sometimes the list of samplers operating on a model represents misplaced computational costs.  A categorical sampler for a node with many categories can be inefficient, and that node may not be a limitation on mixing, so it can work well to use a faster sampler.  Sometimes multiple nodes share identical or nearly identical dependencies (other nodes that depend on them).  This means that the same computational effort is involved in sampling them, and for this reason it can make sense to sample them jointly, such as with RW_block.  Sometimes we can identify parts of a model that can be re-written using nimbleFunctions to provide new functions or distributions in the model.  New functions can combine multiple steps into single steps, reducing the size of the model, which can improve efficiency.  New distributions can be useful to analytically sum or integrate over latent states when it is simple to do so.  The zero-inflated Poisson example on our web site is a simple case.  More complicated cases of doing this for capture-recapture and hidden Markov models are given in Turek et al. (2016; Environ Ecol Stat (2016) 23: 549. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-016-0353-z).  Sometimes changing the parameterization of a model (e.g. from non-centered to centered random effects) or centering explanatory variables can lead to improved mixing.
> > >
> > > -Perry
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thu, Feb 28, 2019 at 6:20 PM Chris Paciorek <christophe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi Manushi,
> > > >
> > > > In general, a few of the tools that NIMBLE provides to help with this are:
> > > >
> > > > 1) trying different samplers for one or more nodes (e.g., switching
> > > > from random walk Metropolis ("RW") samplers to slice samplers or using
> > > > the RW sampler on the log scale). See Sec 7.2 of the NIMBLE manual.
> > > > 2) if the node (i.e. ,parameter) is highly correlated with one or more
> > > > other nodes, blocking nodes together, e.g., with the RW_block sampler.
> > > > There's a bit of an example
> > > > in Section 2.6 of the manual or see the "Customizing an MCMC" and
> > > > "Building a generalized linear mixed model" examples at
> > > > https://r-nimble.org/examples.
> > > > 3) writing your own customized sampler (if you have some idea of how
> > > > to make better proposals for the slow-mixing parameter). See Sec 15.5
> > > > of the manual.
> > > > 4) In some cases, finding better starting values for the MCMC can help.
> > > > 5) Sometimes reparameterizing the model helps, though that is not
> > > > explicitly something that is part of NIMBLE.
> > > >
> > > > Other users might weigh in with strategies that they've used.
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, Feb 28, 2019 at 6:55 AM Manushi Welandawe <man...@my.uri.edu> wrote:

Hi Claudia,

Thank you for your response.

Yeah, I need to replicate the columns of y to match the dimensions:

Another way to write the algorithms is as follows:

library(nimble)
library(rdist)
library(raster)
library(dplyr)

netdist <- read.csv('country_distance.csv')

N <- 64
S <- 64

mybeta <- c(2,2,0, 4, 2)
set.seed(1)
x1 <- rnorm(64);
x2 <- rnorm(64);
x3 <- rnorm(64);
x4 <- rnorm(64);
x5 <- rnorm(64);
y  <- cbind(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5) %*% mybeta + rnorm(64)
y <-  matrix(y, nrow = length(y), ncol = length(y), byrow = FALSE)

library(nimble)

SLMMCode <- nimbleCode({

  for (i in 1:S){
    y[1:N, i] ~ dmnorm(mu_y[1:N, i], prec = tau_y0[1:N, 1:N, i])
    mu_y[1:N, i] <- b[i, 1] * x1[1:N] + b[i, 2] * x2[1:N] + b[i, 3] *
      x3[1:N] + b[i, 4] * x4[1:N] + b[i, 5] * x5[1:N]
    tau_y0[1:N, 1:N, i] <- diag(psi_y[i] * exp(-Dist[1:N, i]/lambda))
    psi_y[i] ~ dgamma(1, 1)

   b[i, 1:5] <- bm[latent[i], 1:5]
    latent[i] ~ dcat(zlatent[1:M])
  }

lambda ~ dunif(0, D)

for (k in 1:M) {

  bm[k, 1:5] ~ dmnorm(mu_bm[1:5], cov = var_bm[1:5, 1:5])
}
var_bm[1:5, 1:5] <- 1/tau_bm * diag(rep(1, 5))
tau_bm ~ dgamma(1, 1)

for (j in 1:5) {
  mu_bm[j] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
}

zlatent[1:M] <- stick_breaking(vlatent[1:(M - 1)])

for (j in 1:(M - 1)) {
  vlatent[j] ~ dbeta(1, alpha)
}

alpha ~ dgamma(1,1)

})

netdist <- read.csv('country_distance.csv')
my_points <- matrix(c(netdist$Longitude,    # Create longitude/latitude matrix
                      netdist$Latitude),ncol=2)

colnames(my_points) <- c("longitude", "latitude")

my_points

# dist_mat <- pdist(my_points)

# generate data

df <- my_points
# distance matrices
dist_mat <- pdist(df)
dist_1 <- pdist(df[, 1])
dist_2 <- pdist(df[, 2])

dist_prod <- product_metric(dist_1, dist_2)
# check equality
all.equal(dist_mat, dist_prod)

GWRData <- list(y = y, x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3 = x3, x4 = x4, x5 = x5,
                Dist = dist_prod)

GWRConst <- list(S = S, M = 50, N = N, D = 50)

GWRInits <- list(psi_y = rep(1, GWRConst$S), lambda = 10,alpha=1,
                 latent = sample(1:50, size = GWRConst$S, replace = TRUE), tau_bm = 1,  mu_bm = rnorm(5), phi = 1,
                 vlatent = rbeta(GWRConst$M - 1, 1, 1),bm=matrix(rnorm(320),nrow = 64,ncol = 5))

mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code = SLMMCode, data = GWRData, constants = GWRConst,

                       inits = GWRInits, niter = 5000, nchains = 1,

                       monitors = c("latent", "lambda",'b','bm'), setSeed = TRUE)

But still, the values of betas did not change too much, even if I increased the number of iterations and changed the level of truncation for the stick-breaking to 50.

Thanks

messages.body_plain:
I am starting to thinking a little more about how to build on the work documented in this thread, one piece of functionality that would be nice to add is to be able to resume sampling from where one has left off if interrupted (e.g., due to a power outage or automatic Windows update). Is it possible to save the entire MCMC sampling state to the hard drive such that one can resume sampling from that point rather than starting from scratch?

On Monday, January 2, 2023 at 4:36:30 PM UTC-7 Quresh Latif wrote:
> Gotcha, that makes sense. Thanks!
>
> On Monday, January 2, 2023 at 4:24:04 PM UTC-7 Christopher Paciorek wrote:
> > Hi Quresh,
> >
> > It's probably picking up the value of `nspp` from a variable named `nspp` in your R global environment when it is not found in `constants`. That variable wouldn't be present in the worker processes, hence the error when parallelizing.
> >
> > In some cases, we've been careful to prevent objects from being found via R's scoping rules, but in this case and some other cases, objects will be found by R's scoping rules if you don't provide them in the usual 'nimble' manner. In this case, it might be better if nimble errored out -- it's something that's been in the back of our minds for a while.
> >
> > -chris
> >
> > On Tue, Dec 27, 2022 at 2:16 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > Well, once I sat down at my desk for real and my brain wasn't in vacation mode, I quickly found the error in my code. I had not included 'nspp' in my list of constants. The 'nspp' object specifies the number of species represented in the data, and thus the length of the species loop for defining the model. Given the bone-headed nature of my mistake, I now feel sheepish posting about it here, except that it's still puzzling why the model ran with 'nimbleMCMC' without throwing an error. I also was able to run the model using the more base set of NIMBLE functions that are embedded within 'RunNimbleParallel' (i.e., nimbleModel, compileNimble, configureMCMC, etc. implemented in lines 24 to 32 in the 'RunNimbleParallel' function). The model and samplers apparently get compiled and run just fine with no errors even though I am missing 'nspp' in my list of constants. Moreover, when I check the model after defining it using the 'nimbleModel' function by running 'model$calculate()', I get a number rather than NA or Inf, so the log-probability appears fully defined despite not having specified the length of the species loop. Curious if there are any insights out there as to why I only get an error with this mistake when attempting parallel processing.
> > >
> > > On Sunday, December 25, 2022 at 1:30:25 PM UTC-7 Quresh Latif wrote:
> > > > Hi all. I have run into a headscratcher with the parallel processing function that I wrote and posted in this thread. I am trying to run a zero-inflated dynamic community abundance model. The model runs fine with 'nimbleMCMC', but when I try to run it using ' RunNimbleParallel' function, I get the following error:
> > > >
> > > > "Error in checkForRemoteErrors(lapply(cl, recvResult)) : 2 nodes produced errors; first error: Could not evaluate loop syntax: is indexing information provided via 'constants'?"

messages.subject: Different initial values for each chain
messages.subject_clean: Different initial values for each chain
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm sorry if this has been documented elsewhere but I haven't been able to find it. I'm wondering, what's the best way to set new initial values for each chain? If I'm understanding correctly, using a function for initial values in nimbleModel() only uses fresh values for the first chain, where the subsequent chains start where the previous one left off. I think using a initial values in runMCMC() does start new initial values, but only for those nodes where a new initial values are assigned. I've been using that method, but for subsequent chains I always get a bunch of error messages for some nodes. I think this is due to my new initial values corresponding some of the nodes that aren't reset contradicting those nodes. I think nimble does a good job of fixing these errors after the first iteration, but it'd be nice not to get them at all, and I'm sure things won't always go smoothly.

Is there a way to start fully "fresh" MCMC chains, where any nodes that aren't provided initial values are simulated by nimble, using runMCMC()?

Thanks!

Matt

messages.body_plain:
I found this thread because I am (was) getting the exact same message, and it looks to me like the error message is incorrect.  Alex already has `x` specified as a vector in the `dar1` distribution, and does have `Y[i,1:m]` in the model code.  And  I also do have `x = double(1)` specified in my custom distribution, and I do specify a vector value on the left-hand side of the tilde in the model code.

When I ran Alex's code

```

Rcode <- nimbleCode({
  # likelihood ==============
  for(i in 1:N) Y[i,1:m] ~ dar1(sigma=sigma0[i],rho=rho0[i])
  # process =================
  for (i in 1:N) sigma0[i] ~ dunif(0.01,max(sigma.all))
  for (i in 1:N) rho0[i] ~ dunif(-0.999,0.999)
})

```
it generated the Dimension error as described.

But when I skipped the  `registerDistributions` bit, and then ran the `Rmodel <- nimbleModel(` piece, it did NOT generate the error, but generated a message that `NIMBLE has registered dar1 as a distribution based on its use in BUGS code.` There were other errors upon compilation, and the compilation failed. I won't comment on the model itself, but I am really curious why running  `registerDistributions` generates and error message that seems incorrect. As Chris points out, it seems like `registerDistributions` is not necessary, but it seems to cause a problem. Am I missing something?

As an aside, when I tried skipping  `registerDistributions` for my case, I was able to build the model without generating the error.  Also, I'll note that when I tried a version of this distribution where x was specified as scalar, then `registerDistributions` did not seem to be a problem.

Thanks,
Glenn

> Hi Alex,
>
> Regarding the error message, that is referring to the fact that 'x' should be a vector not a scalar, so you need `x = double(1)` when defining `dar1`.
> We should clarify that error message - I've made a note for us to do that.
>
> Also, you'll need  `Y[i,1:m]` in your model code.
> And as a side note, you don't need `rar1` or `registerDistributions`, though it's ok to have them. As you have it ,`rar1` is not consistent with `dar1` as it returns a scalar, but it's just a placeholder, so it's ok.

> Apart from that it should work from a mechanical perspective. Perhaps others will comment on your modeling question - it's a broad question and there are lots of things one can do with spatio-temporal data like this - allowing for spatial structure in 'y' or in 'sigma' or in 'rho'.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have downloaded the beta version from (https://r-nimble.org/ad-beta) to be able to estimate parameters via HMC. Everything worked wonderful, though last week I was getting a compilation error when trying to compile my model.

After searching a long time for the source of the error I hope to have finally found the problem. It looks like the model does not compile when adding a Nimble function to the parameters and setting the option buildDerivs=TRUE.

Below I created a reproducible dummy example (not my actual code) that shows the problem.

The dummy model is the following:

Y_ij = intercept + u_i + v_j + eps_ij         with i = j = 1,…,20.

Where u_i and v_j are constraint to sum-to-zero, making the intercept identifiable.

For notational clarity I wrote a separate function which does the trick.

SumToZero <- nimbleFunction( #Function to Sum Vector to Zero

  run = function(x = double(1)){ #input Vector

    returnType(double(1))

    n <- length(x)

    xbar <- mean(x)

    xtilde <- numeric(n, init=FALSE)

    for(i in 1:n){

      xtilde[i] <- x[i]-xbar

    }

    return(xtilde)

  }

)

ExampleCode <- nimbleCode({

  intercept ~ dnorm(0,sd=10)

  for(i in 1:I){

    u[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)

    v[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)

  }

   utilde[1:I] <- SumToZero(u[1:I])

   vtilde[1:J] <- SumToZero(v[1:J])

  sigma ~ dunif(0,5)

  for(i in 1:n){

    predicted_mu[i] <- intercept + utilde[IInd[i]]+vtilde[JInd[i]]

    y[i] ~ dnorm(mean=predicted_mu[i], sd= sigma)

  }

})

I then created some simulated data

set.seed(124)

u <- rnorm(20,mean = 1,sd = 2)

v <- rnorm(20,mean = 3,sd = 3)

utilde <- u- mean(u)

vtilde <- v-mean(v)

Indicies <- expand.grid("IInd"=1:20, "JInd"=1:20)

intercept <- 10

YData <- rnorm(n=400, mean = intercept +

                 utilde[Indicies$IInd]+

                 vtilde[Indicies$JInd], sd=1)

### Creating Constants and Data

Const <- list("n"=400,

              "I"=20,

              "J"=20,

              "IInd"=Indicies$IInd,

              "JInd"=Indicies$JInd)

Data <- list("y"=YData)

TestModel <- nimbleModel(code=ExampleCode,

                         constants = Const,

                         data=Data,

                         inits = Inits(),

                         buildDerivs = TRUE)

## Configuration and model building is skipped for brevity

cModel <- compileNimble(TestModel,showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

which results in the following error

Error: Failed to create the shared library. (I have also added the compiler output)

When setting the option to buildDerivs=FALSE, no error occurs.

Interestingly, the model compiles fine when incorporating the sum-to-zero constraint in the model code, i.e. not as a separate NIMBLE function.

Compiling the following code and setting a HMC sampler on u, respectively v works just fine.

ExampleCode2 <- nimbleCode({

  intercept ~ dnorm(0,sd=10)

  for(i in 1:I){

    u[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)

    v[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)

  }

   umean <- mean(u[1:I])

   vmean <- mean(v[1:J])

   for(i in 1:I){

     utilde[i] <- u[i]-umean

     vtilde[i] <- v[i]-vmean

   }

  sigma ~ dunif(0,5)

  for(i in 1:n){

    predicted_mu[i] <- intercept + utilde[IInd[i]]+vtilde[JInd[i]]

    y[i] ~ dnorm(mean=predicted_mu[i], sd= sigma)

  }

})

TestModel2 <- nimbleModel(code=ExampleCode2,

                         constants = Const,

                         data=Data,

                         inits = Inits(),

                         buildDerivs = TRUE)

#works fine

cModel2 <- compileNimble(TestModel2,

                        showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

I am using the newest version of R (4.2.2) and have downloaded rtools42. Below you can find my session Info:

Anyone knows the root of the problem? Help is very much appreciated.

In addition, I have noticed that model building and compilation time increases a lot (around 2000%) when adding a fairly complex linear transformation to my parameters. That is, for a different model my vectors of parameters (let’s say u and v) need to be orthogonal to each other.

I therefore implemented a gram-schmidt orthogonalization process on both u and v and calculate an orthogonal projection to create a new vtilde that is orthogonal to u (Parameters are sampled for u and v). Incorporation this transformation increases my model building time from around 3 seconds to around 70 seconds. Is this normal ?

Thanks in advance for all your help!

messages.body_plain:
Queresh, good question.  The short answer is there's no built-in mechanism for doing this in NIMBLE's MCMC, but there have been two attempts at documenting the procedure you're asking about.  I think the second of these is a little better, but please take a look at both:

http://danielturek.github.io/public/restartingMCMC/restartingMCMC.html
https://danielturek.github.io/public/saveMCMCstate/saveMCMCstate.html

Let me know if you have any questions about this.

Cheers,
Daniel

On Mon, Jan 23, 2023 at 12:08 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:

> I am starting to thinking a little more about how to build on the work documented in this thread, one piece of functionality that would be nice to add is to be able to resume sampling from where one has left off if interrupted (e.g., due to a power outage or automatic Windows update). Is it possible to save the entire MCMC sampling state to the hard drive such that one can resume sampling from that point rather than starting from scratch?
>
> On Monday, January 2, 2023 at 4:36:30 PM UTC-7 Quresh Latif wrote:
> > Gotcha, that makes sense. Thanks!
> >
> > On Monday, January 2, 2023 at 4:24:04 PM UTC-7 Christopher Paciorek wrote:
> > > Hi Quresh,
> > >
> > > It's probably picking up the value of `nspp` from a variable named `nspp` in your R global environment when it is not found in `constants`. That variable wouldn't be present in the worker processes, hence the error when parallelizing.
> > >
> > > In some cases, we've been careful to prevent objects from being found via R's scoping rules, but in this case and some other cases, objects will be found by R's scoping rules if you don't provide them in the usual 'nimble' manner. In this case, it might be better if nimble errored out -- it's something that's been in the back of our minds for a while.
> > >
> > > -chris
> > >
> > > On Tue, Dec 27, 2022 at 2:16 PM Quresh Latif <quresh...@birdconservancy.org> wrote:
> > > > Well, once I sat down at my desk for real and my brain wasn't in vacation mode, I quickly found the error in my code. I had not included 'nspp' in my list of constants. The 'nspp' object specifies the number of species represented in the data, and thus the length of the species loop for defining the model. Given the bone-headed nature of my mistake, I now feel sheepish posting about it here, except that it's still puzzling why the model ran with 'nimbleMCMC' without throwing an error. I also was able to run the model using the more base set of NIMBLE functions that are embedded within 'RunNimbleParallel' (i.e., nimbleModel, compileNimble, configureMCMC, etc. implemented in lines 24 to 32 in the 'RunNimbleParallel' function). The model and samplers apparently get compiled and run just fine with no errors even though I am missing 'nspp' in my list of constants. messages.body_plain:
Following up after we found a solution to this:

Chris kindly worked me through several work-arounds that didn't resolve the error, and he thought it was probably an issue with how gcc was installed on the supercomputer nodes. Tech support for the supercomputer was initially mystified because "features.h" appeared to be in the right place, but eventually they figured out that that appearance was deceiving (something to do with the "provisioning system"). I'm not familiar with the technical details, but they said, "Essentially the system that plops the OS on the nodes claimed all files are intact on the nodes, but in some cases and on some nodes, it lied. I just forced a reinstalled of some headers ... the features.h file was actually in /usr/include."

After that reinstall of the headers, NIMBLE runs just fine on the nodes that were previously failing.

Hopefully this was a one-off odd issue that won't come up for any of you in the future, but there's a record of the solution for posterity!

Thanks,

Emily

messages.body_plain:
A couple additional comments here:

1) The error when using `registerDistributions` is because the `types` argument doesn't specify "value = double(1)". By default it will treat the density value as being scalar if it's not specified. `registerDistributions` does not mix and match `types` information that can be gleaned from the actual 'd' function with what is provided as input to `registerDistributions`.

2) The model code has `max(sigma.all)`, which won't compile because `sigma.all` is a scalar. (As a side note, `sigma.all` is never specified anywhere but that is just a matter of providing values to the model and wouldn't cause a compilation error.)  It looks like we need to do a better job of error-trapping (or allowing) code where `max` or `min` is applied to a scalar -- I'm filing an issue for us to take a look at that.

I think that addresses the various issues raised in this thread, but let me know if there are further questions/problems.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Julius,

Thanks for the question and the clear, reproducible (and simplified) code.

You need to provide a buildDerivs argument to the nimbleFunction call that creates SumToZero.  In this case, you also need to tell it that "i" is not a variable for derivative tracking, so please try:

 buildDerivs = list(run = list(ignore = 'i'))

An alternative is to do i <- 0L prior to the for loop, which clearly establishes for the compiler that i is to be an integer and thus be definition not have derivative tracking.  If you do that, you can replace the above with simply

buildDerivs = TRUE
or
buildDerivs = 'run'

BTW, in either your SumToZero or your version that does it in the model code, you should be able to use a vectorized statement.  In SumToZero, this should work:
 xtilde <- x-mean(x)

In the model code, you would need explicit indexing, so

utilde[1:I] <- u[1:I]-mean(u[1:I])

Great to see you trying HMC and post more questions if needed.  We are working towards regular (non-beta) release of the AD features.  I believe we are adding an error-trap for missing buildDerivs arguments in models or nimbleFunctions where they seem to be intended.  However, error-trapping for issues like the need for "ignore='i'" is a substantially harder challenge and likely to remain rudimentary for a while.

HTH!
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

Thanks for the question.  I think I follow what you're saying.  The MCMC initializer (called as almost the very first step of running an MCMC) will draw values for nodes that are NA from their priors.  I think you could get the behavior you want if the inits you provide to runMCMC (whether as a list or a function) puts NAs in the nodes that you want drawn freshly from their priors (after other inits values are assigned).

(For full control, you could skip runMCMC and set up the model's values however you like and then call mcmc$run(...), but I'm assuming you'd prefer to stick with runMCMC.)

HTH!
Perry

> Hi Javier,

>
> library(nimble)

>     r <- sum(b[1:n] <= b[s]) # This is what rank(b, s) in BUGS does, I think

> m$b <- rnorm(10)
> m$s <- 3
> m$calculate('r')
> m$r   # Here is the answer calculated in the model
> rank(m$b)[m$s]  # Here is the answer calculated directly in R.  They match.
>
> # Test it compiled
> cm <- compileNimble(m)
> cm$calculate('r')
> cm$r  # Here is the answer calculated in the compiled model.
>
> If you want to try writing versions yourself, usually the easiest place to start is with a nimbleFunction.  E.g.
>
> myrank <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x = double(1), i = double()) {
>     ans <- 0
>     val <- x[i]
>     for(j in 1:length(x))
>       ans <- ans + (x[j] <= val)
>     return(ans)
>     returnType(double())
>   }
> )
>

>   nimbleCode({
>     r <- myrank(b[1:n], s)
>   }),

>
> set.seed(100)
> m$b <- rnorm(10)
> m$s <- 3

>
> cm <- compileNimble(m)

> cm$r
>

messages.subject_clean: Updating tau in dcar_normal
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was fitting an improper CAR model with a gamma prior for tau and noticed that it was updated using RW Sampler. I'd assumed that tau would show up as a conjugate sampler. A small example code is below (actually the one in the NIMBLE user manual). I would appreciate it if anyone could share any thoughts or ideas.

> # Improper
> code <- nimbleCode({
+         alpha ~ dflat()
+         beta ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)
+         tau ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
+         s[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:N], tau, zero_mean = 1)
+         for(i in 1:N) {
+                 log(lambda[i]) <- alpha + beta*x[i] + s[i]
+                 y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
+         }
+ })
>
> L <- 8
> constants <- list(N = 4, L = L, num = c(3, 2, 2, 1), weights = rep(1, L),
+                   adj = c(2,3,4,1,3,1,2,1), x = c(0, 2, 2, 8))
> data <- list(y = c(6, 9, 7, 12))
> inits <- list(alpha = 0, beta = 0, tau = 1, s = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
> Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)
Defining model
Building model
Setting data and initial values
Running calculate on model
  [Note] Any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables.
Checking model sizes and dimensions
>
> compiled_mod <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
===== Monitors =====
thin = 1: alpha, beta, tau
===== Samplers =====
RW sampler (3)
  - alpha
  - beta
  - tau
CAR_normal sampler (1)
  - s[1:4]

Thank you!
Ji

> Hi Julius,

>
> You need to provide a buildDerivs argument to the nimbleFunction call that creates SumToZero.  In this case, you also need to tell it that "i" is not a variable for derivative tracking, so please try:
>
>  buildDerivs = list(run = list(ignore = 'i'))
>
> An alternative is to do i <- 0L prior to the for loop, which clearly establishes for the compiler that i is to be an integer and thus be definition not have derivative tracking.  If you do that, you can replace the above with simply
>
> buildDerivs = TRUE
> or
> buildDerivs = 'run'
>
> BTW, in either your SumToZero or your version that does it in the model code, you should be able to use a vectorized statement.  In SumToZero, this should work:
>  xtilde <- x-mean(x)
>
> In the model code, you would need explicit indexing, so
>
> utilde[1:I] <- u[1:I]-mean(u[1:I])
>
> Great to see you trying HMC and post more questions if needed.  We are working towards regular (non-beta) release of the AD features.  I believe we are adding an error-trap for missing buildDerivs arguments in models or nimbleFunctions where they seem to be intended. > Perry

messages.body_plain:
Good question, Julius.  The answer is that delta = 0.65 is the value recommended in Hoffman and Gelman (2014), which appears in section 3.2.3.

Note, however, you can easily change this value in nimble's HMC sampler using any of the following:

conf <- configureMCMC(model)
conf$addSampler(target = nodeNames, type = "HMC", delta = 0.8)

or

conf <- configureMCMC(model)
addHMC(conf, nodes = nodeNames, control = list(delta = 0.8))

or

conf <- configureHMC(model, delta = 0.8)

This would easily facilitate experimenting with what values of delta work well, in different modelling situations.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Another update on this. Turns out I had an error in my model, which ultimately explains the poor mixing. I had the following:

log(r) <- delta0 + deltaVec * X
Nt <- exp(r) * N(t-1)

Thus, I was multiplying prior year N by a log-scale parameter rather than on the real scale.

So, I should have checked my model before thinking about how to optimize sampling seeing chains like this.

On Thursday, January 19, 2023 at 4:38:21 PM UTC-7 Quresh Latif wrote:
> Is it typical for the intercept and covariate parameters for a given demographic parameter to be correlated and therefore good candidates for trying a RW_block sampler to sample them together?
>
> I have an exponential growth parameter, r, in a population model that I am relating with covariates using a log link function:
>
> log(r[g, (t-1)]) <- delta0 + inprod(deltaVec[1:n.Xdelta], Xdelta.array[g, t, 1:n.Xdelta]), where g indexes site and t indexes year.
>
> I've got a couple traceplot (after applying some burnin and thinning) shown in the attached images, one for the intercept (delta0) and the other for the 12th covariate (delta12). The traceplots for the other covariate parameters look similar where the black chain looks to be mixing reasonably well but the red one is struggling. Considering these, does it seem like the log-linear regression parameters for r are likely correlated and would benefit from an RW_block sampler?
>
> Also, I am currently using adaptation. I'm wondering if there's a way to record the tuning values ('scale' in the configureMCMC function?) or if that is automatically recorded somewhere. If so, would it help to identify what scale has arrived at for the black chain and then fix it to that value from the beginning for both chains? Along with that, is it possible to set 'scale' to different values for different parameters, or somehow tune the samplers for different parameters differently?
>
> I am still working through the section of the user manual on this, so apologies for taking up space here if this is all spelled out there.
>
> On Friday, March 1, 2019 at 9:47:36 AM UTC-7 pdevalpine wrote:
> > I'll add some strategies to what Chris wrote.
> >
> > Sometimes the list of samplers operating on a model represents misplaced computational costs.  A categorical sampler for a node with many categories can be inefficient, and that node may not be a limitation on mixing, so it can work well to use a faster sampler.  Sometimes multiple nodes share identical or nearly identical dependencies (other nodes that depend on them).  This means that the same computational effort is involved in sampling them, and for this reason it can make sense to sample them jointly, such as with RW_block.  Sometimes we can identify parts of a model that can be re-written using nimbleFunctions to provide new functions or distributions in the model.  New functions can combine multiple steps into single steps, reducing the size of the model, which can improve efficiency.  New distributions can be useful to analytically sum or integrate over latent states when it is simple to do so.  The zero-inflated Poisson example on our web site is a simple case.  More complicated cases of doing this for capture-recapture and hidden Markov models are given in Turek et al. (2016; Environ Ecol Stat (2016) 23: 549. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10651-016-0353-z).  Sometimes changing the parameterization of a model (e.g. from non-centered to centered random effects) or centering explanatory variables can lead to improved mixing.
> >
> > -Perry
> >
> >
> > On Thu, Feb 28, 2019 at 6:20 PM Chris Paciorek <christophe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi Manushi,
> > >
> > > In general, a few of the tools that NIMBLE provides to help with this are:
> > >
> > > 1) trying different samplers for one or more nodes (e.g., switching
> > > from random walk Metropolis ("RW") samplers to slice samplers or using
> > > the RW sampler on the log scale). See Sec 7.2 of the NIMBLE manual.
> > > 2) if the node (i.e. ,parameter) is highly correlated with one or more
> > > other nodes, blocking nodes together, e.g., with the RW_block sampler.
> > > There's a bit of an example
> > > in Section 2.6 of the manual or see the "Customizing an MCMC" and
> > > "Building a generalized linear mixed model" examples at
> > > https://r-nimble.org/examples.
> > > 3) writing your own customized sampler (if you have some idea of how
> > > to make better proposals for the slow-mixing parameter). See Sec 15.5
> > > of the manual.
> > > 4) In some cases, finding better starting values for the MCMC can help.
> > > 5) Sometimes reparameterizing the model helps, though that is not
> > > explicitly something that is part of NIMBLE.
> > >
> > > Other users might weigh in with strategies that they've used.
> > >
> > > On Thu, Feb 28, 2019 at 6:55 AM Manushi Welandawe <man...@my.uri.edu> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi All,
> > > >
> > > > I would like to know the techniques that I can use in nimble to improve the convergence of the MCMC samples.
> > > >
> > > > Thank you
> > > >
> > > > Best,
> > > > Manushi

Hi all,

Pardon me if this isn't necessarily a nimble issue.

I'm interested in running a big model in parallel using the instructions on the nimble website. The model I want to use it for uses huge amounts of RAM and nearly maxes out the machine we're using. Most of this RAM use comes up during buildMCMC() and subsequently compileNimble(); the RAM use is quite manageable during the MCMC sampling. I'm assuming here that running these steps in parallel will increase the RAM use of the machine.

Is it possible to do the model and MCMC building sequentially, while doing the MCMC step in parallel?

Thanks!

Matt

code <- nimbleCode({
  Omega[1:p,1:p] ~ dwish(R[1:p,1:p], 20)

messages.subject: Re: Warning: value in right-hand-side-only variable is NA or NaN
messages.subject_clean: Warning: value in right-hand-side-only variable is NA or NaN
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dali,

Before opening up your code, let me more quickly offer suggestions for how you can debug this issue yourself.  A right-hand-side only variable is a variable that appears only on the right-hand side of model declarations and never on the left-hand side.  This is often the case for explanatory variables.  For example, in

a ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
b ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
for(i in 1:n) {
y[i] ~ dnorm(a + b*x[i], sd = sigma)
}

x[i] is a right-hand-side only variable because it is used as an explanatory variable but does not itself have a prior or a deterministic declaration.

You can use the model object to determine where you have NA or NaN values.  Build the model with nimbleModel.  (If you have been using nimbleMCMC to skip over nimbleModel, simply use the same code, data, constants, and/or inits in a call to nimbleModel, with the exception that inits can't be set up for multiple chains but should rather be a list of named model variables.)

Then, inspect variables in your model.  For example,

model <- nimbleModel(code, data = data, constants = constants, inits = inits) # same arguments as nimbleMCMC
model$x # look at x

In this way you can identify which variables contain NAs and/or NaNs.  Often it means that the data or constants are incomplete or incorrectly set up.

Can you please try these approaches (or let us know if you already have) and then if you are still stuck let us know and someone can run your code?

If you haven't yet dug into our user manual at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>, that can also be a helpful source.

HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Here's one idea. Set it up to do it in parallel, but in your function that is run in parallel include a Sys.sleep() call that is set up so that the different chains are offset in terms of when the memory-intensity steps start.

Alternatively run the chains in completely independent R sessions and make sure to offset the starting times as needed.

-Chris

messages.subject: Re: Missing data in multinomial distribution
messages.subject_clean: Missing data in multinomial distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Abby,

I took a look at this. I also was confused by the error message but this syntax in your nimblefunction calc_cond_prob caught my eye:

          array[t,j,i] <- if(is.na <http://is.na>(obs_ref[t,j,i])){ .......

I tried changing the contents of the nimbleFunction to do the assignment inside the if-statements and it seems to work now. I'm pasting the full nimbleFunction below. I have a feeling that in base-R the syntax x <- if(cond) {} is doing something fancy that NIMBLE doesn't support.

Hope this solves the problem--
Ben

calc_cond_prob <- nimbleFunction(
  #input and output types

  run = function(nsite = double(0), # scalar
                 ntime = double(0), # scalar
                 nobs = double(0), # scalar
                 obs_ref = double(3),  # array

                 p_m = double(0), #scalar
                 p_f = double(0), # scalar

                 no_m = double(2), # matrix
                 no_f = double(2)) #matrix
  {
    returnType(double(3))  # array return

    # Conditional multinomial cell probabilities -- trap level
    #create empty array
    array <- array(NA,dim=c(ntime,nobs,nsite))
    #loop through sites, visits, observations

    for(i in 1:nsite){
      for(t in 1:ntime){
        for(j in 1:nobs){

          array[t,j,i] <- if(is.na <http://is.na>(obs_ref[t,j,i])){
            0
          } else if(obs_ref[t,j,i]==2){ #removal type m

            p_m / (no_m[t,i]*p_m+no_f[t,i]*p_f)

          } else if(obs_ref[t,j,i]==1){ #removal type f

            p_f / (no_m[t,i]*p_m+no_f[t,i]*p_f)
          }
        }
      }
    }

    return(array[1:ntime,1:nobs,1:nsite])
  }
)

messages.body_plain:
Oops, I copy/pasted the unedited version. Here's the version that worked for me.

calc_cond_prob <- nimbleFunction(
  #input and output types
  run = function(nsite = double(0), # scalar
                 ntime = double(0), # scalar
                 nobs = double(0), # scalar
                 obs_ref = double(3),  # array
                 p_m = double(0), #scalar
                 p_f = double(0), # scalar
                 no_m = double(2), # matrix
                 no_f = double(2)) #matrix
  {
    returnType(double(3))  # array return

    # Conditional multinomial cell probabilities -- trap level
    #create empty array
    array <- array(NA,dim=c(ntime,nobs,nsite))
    #loop through sites, visits, observations
    for(i in 1:nsite){
      for(t in 1:ntime){
        for(j in 1:nobs){

          if (is.na <http://is.na>(obs_ref[t,j,i])){
            array[t,j,i] <- 0

          } else if(obs_ref[t,j,i]==2){ #removal type m

            array[t,j,i] <- p_m / (no_m[t,i]*p_m+no_f[t,i]*p_f)

          } else if(obs_ref[t,j,i]==1){ #removal type f

            array[t,j,i] <- p_f / (no_m[t,i]*p_m+no_f[t,i]*p_f)

          }
        }
      }
    }
    return(array[1:ntime,1:nobs,1:nsite])
  }
)

> Dear Dali,
>
> Before opening up your code, let me more quickly offer suggestions for how you can debug this issue yourself.  A right-hand-side only variable is a variable that appears only on the right-hand side of model declarations and never on the left-hand side.  This is often the case for explanatory variables.  For example, in
>
> a ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
> b ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
> sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)
> for(i in 1:n) {
> y[i] ~ dnorm(a + b*x[i], sd = sigma)
> }
>
> x[i] is a right-hand-side only variable because it is used as an explanatory variable but does not itself have a prior or a deterministic declaration.
>
> You can use the model object to determine where you have NA or NaN values.  Build the model with nimbleModel.  (If you have been using nimbleMCMC to skip over nimbleModel, simply use the same code, data, constants, and/or inits in a call to nimbleModel, with the exception that inits can't be set up for multiple chains but should rather be a list of named model variables.)
>
> Then, inspect variables in your model.  For example,
>
> model <- nimbleModel(code, data = data, constants = constants, inits = inits) # same arguments as nimbleMCMC
> model$x # look at x
>
> In this way you can identify which variables contain NAs and/or NaNs.  Often it means that the data or constants are incomplete or incorrectly set up.
>
> Can you please try these approaches (or let us know if you already have) and then if you are still stuck let us know and someone can run your code?
>
> If you haven't yet dug into our user manual at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>, that can also be a helpful source.
>
> HTH
> Perry

messages.subject: Errors in sampler selection leads to failed MCMC
messages.subject_clean: Errors in sampler selection leads to failed MCMC
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Sorry for the two posts in two days.

I am trying to run the following model, which compiles fine but gives an error in the MCMC.

code <- nimbleCode({
  for(j in 1:p){
    w[1:n, j] ~ dmnorm(zeroes[1:n], cov = cov[1:n, 1:n])
  }
  for(i in 1:n){
    y[i, 1:p] ~ dmnorm(w[i, 1:p], cov = Omega[1:p, 1:p])
  }
})

# constants
{
  cov <- structure(c(1, 0.291439908378029, 0.944925896806776, 0.291439908378029,
                     1, 0.278127103103443, 0.944925896806776, 0.278127103103443, 1
  ), dim = c(3L, 3L))
  n <- 3; p <- 2

  constants <- list(Omega = diag(1,p),
                    zeroes = rep(0, n),
                    p = p,
                    n = n,
                    cov = cov)

}

jsdmModel <- nimbleModel(code,
                         constants = constants)

jsdmModel$setData(list(y = matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)))

jsdmcompiled <- compileNimble(jsdmModel, resetFunctions = T)
jsdmConf <- configureMCMC(jsdmcompiled, print = TRUE,
                          enableWAIC = T)
jsdmMCMC <- buildMCMC(jsdmConf)
CDNAMCMC <- compileNimble(jsdmMCMC)
MCMCsamples <- runMCMC(CDNAMCMC, niter = 10000, WAIC = T)

The last step gives the error:
Run-time size error: expected dim(prior_prec)[1] == dim(contribution_mean)[1]
Error in mapCopy.  Sizes don't match: 3 != 2

I am not an expert, but I think that the error comes from the selected sampler for w[1:n,j], since it comes out as conjugate even though it shouldn't be.

Indeed, by removing the sampler for w and replacing it with single RW samplers, the error disappears.

jsdmConf$removeSamplers("w")
jsdmConf$addSampler(target = "w[1,1]", type = "RW")
jsdmConf$addSampler(target = "w[2,1]", type = "RW")
jsdmConf$addSampler(target = "w[1,2]", type = "RW")
jsdmConf$addSampler(target = "w[2,2]", type = "RW")
jsdmConf$addSampler(target = "w[3,1]", type = "RW")
jsdmConf$addSampler(target = "w[3,2]", type = "RW")

Is it a bug of Nimble or am I doing something wrong?

Thanks in advance,

Alex
